storm.summary_layperson: A line of strong thunderstorms is approaching from the west and expected to reach the cove around 8 PM tonight — no cooling effect from Long Island Sound will weaken them here, so conditions will be as intense as those striking nearby towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Long Island Sound water (75°F) is nearly as warm as the air (77°F), leaving no cooling marine layer to weaken tonight's incoming storms.
storm.detail_html:
A line of thunderstorms is approaching from the west, currently stretching 17–30 miles out at 6:37 PM. The leading cell (39 dBZ, 15.5 mi west) is the weakest in the line; the core — cells reaching 54–64 dBZ — is tracked 21–29 miles west. The entire system is moving due east at 8.5 knots, putting the leading edge at the cove around 8 PM (window 7:43–8:41 PM), with the heavier core following roughly 30–50 minutes behind.

Atmospheric instability (CAPE) is at 1,700 J/kg, above the threshold where convection produces strong wind gusts, heavy rain, and lightning. Bulk wind shear is a moderate 14 knots — enough to organize the line but not extreme. NWS Upton has an active Flood Watch through Tuesday morning, reflecting the heavy rain potential with tonight's and tomorrow's storms.

No local mitigating factors are in play tonight. Long Island Sound water temperature is 75°F versus an air temperature of 77°F — a difference of only 2°F. This near-zero air-water gap means no meaningful marine stable layer is present. The Sound is providing no cooling buffer, and the cove will experience storms at roughly the same intensity as surrounding towns.

The storm approach from the west-southwest is the classic perpendicular angle to the Sound — in theory the geometry where the Sound can deflect or weaken incoming cells — but without a stable marine layer to interact with, that geometry is academic tonight. Conditions here will track closely with what the broader metro area sees.

What would change the call: if the line weakens before reaching the coast, or if storm motion shifts toward the northeast routing the strongest cells over the open Sound, risk here would drop. As of this update, motion is tracking due east with no significant change flagged.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked leading cell 15.5 mi west closing at 8.5 kt; a stronger line (54–64 dBZ) follows 20–29 mi out with arrival from 8:35 PM onward.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — southerly synoptic flow, no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: veering S, strengthening ahead of storm line
storm arrival window — outflow gusts exceed model, direction chaotic

wind.tactics_blurb: On this moderate gradient-wind evening — southerly synoptic flow, not a sea-breeze day — the right (west) side of upwind legs carries more pressure during the 5–7 PM window. After 7:30 PM, the approaching storm line makes on-water activity potentially dangerous; thunderstorm outflow gusts during the 7:30–9:30 PM window will substantially exceed what any hourly forecast model shows.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a moderate gradient wind day — the southerly flow is synoptic (weather-pattern driven), not a sea breeze. The air-water temperature difference of 2.2°F (air warmer than water) did not meet the gate needed for a thermal sea breeze to establish, so the sea-breeze maturation direction correction does not apply. HRRR forecast directions are used as-is; current RYC (SSE 157°, 5.3 kt at 6:37 PM) aligns closely with the model's 160° call for this hour.

Coastal stations report a consistent southerly gradient: KBDR (Bridgeport) at 9 kt SSW, the western LIS buoy at 11 kt S with 15 kt gusts, and RYC at 5 kt SSE with 11 kt gusts. APRS land stations in the area read 0–3 kt — sheltered residential sites not representative of open-water speeds. The METAR and RYC readings are the authoritative reference for on-water conditions tonight.

With wind from SSE to S (160–182°) in the pre-storm window, the open southern mouth of Greenwich Cove channels flow from slightly right of center. Pressure sits on the right (west) side of upwind legs — start mid-line and work right on the first beat. Direction variability of ±10–15° is expected as the gradient oscillates ahead of the approaching front.

The window splits into two distinct periods. From 17:00–19:00, expect 6–10 knots of clean southerly gradient with modest gusts — genuine racing breeze. From 19:30 onward, the approaching storm line transforms conditions: outflow winds ahead of the cells can shift rapidly and back to SSW or southwest, and gusts during the storm passage (estimated 7:45–9:30 PM) will significantly exceed HRRR model values. The model shows 8–10 kt sustained through this period, but individual thunderstorm outflow can produce 20–35 kt gusts that no hourly grid model captures. Gust estimates in the 20:00 row reflect elevated storm-outflow potential, not raw HRRR output.

Sunset is at 8:17 PM, but on a gradient-wind evening there is no thermal sea-breeze collapse to manage. The wind transition tonight is driven by the storm passage, not the setting sun. After the line clears (estimated 9:00–9:30 PM), expect a brief post-storm SSW surge followed by settling to 5 kt or less from the south by 10 PM.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 observation 82 minutes old — over-water wind and SST readings may not reflect current conditions.
APRS land-station average speed (1.4 kt) diverges sharply from METAR coastal average (8.1 kt) — sheltered residential sites undercount wind; METAR and RYC used for speed reference.
Sea-breeze maturation direction correction not applied — gradient-wind day (air-water delta 2.2°F below threshold); HRRR forecast directions used as-is.
20:00 gust estimate (22 kt) reflects storm-outflow potential; HRRR model output for that hour shows only 8 kt sustained and does not resolve convective gusts.
